passages.title: The Crowd Within
passages.passage:
A. It is a humbling thought that the body you call your own is, by cell count, only about half human. The remainder is a shifting population of bacteria, fungi and viruses, the great majority of them crowded into the large intestine, and together they are known as the microbiome. For most of medical history these residents were regarded, when they were regarded at all, as passengers at best and stowaways at worst. Only in the last two decades, as the cost of reading genetic material has collapsed, have researchers been able to take a census of the crowd, and what they have found has unsettled some long-held assumptions about where the boundary of a person lies.

B. Far from being idle, the gut's inhabitants earn their keep. They break down fibres that human enzymes cannot touch, manufacture vitamins the body does not make for itself, and train the immune system to tell a genuine threat from a harmless visitor. Some of the chemicals they release travel along the nerve that links the gut to the brain, which is why a growing number of scientists suspect that mood, appetite and even the quality of sleep are partly negotiated in the intestine. Not until a colony is disturbed does its contribution become obvious: a single course of broad-spectrum antibiotics can thin the population dramatically, and it may take months for the original balance to reassert itself, if it ever does.

C. Where does this internal ecosystem come from? Nobody is born with one. A newborn acquires its first residents during birth and in the weeks that follow, from the parents' skin, from milk, from the household and, later, from food and from the soil under its fingernails. The pattern laid down in those early months appears remarkably persistent, which has led some researchers to argue that the first thousand days of life represent a window during which the microbiome is unusually open to influence, for better or worse.

D. Inevitably, so intriguing a story has attracted people eager to sell it. Shelves now groan under supplements promising to "restore" gut health, and diets are marketed with the confidence of a science that is, in truth, still in its infancy. The difficulty is that a healthy microbiome has never been defined. Two perfectly well people may carry communities that barely overlap, and a microbe that is benign in one host may be troublesome in another. Most of the striking results so far come from mice, whose guts and diets bear only a loose resemblance to ours, and the handful of human trials have been small, short and hard to reproduce.

E. None of this makes the field a fraud; it makes it young. The sensible conclusion is not that we should ignore the crowd within, but that we should be wary of anyone claiming to command it. What the evidence does support is unglamorous: a varied diet rich in plants, fewer needless antibiotics, and a certain tolerance for dirt. Had our great-grandparents been told that the secret of good health was to eat vegetables and go outside, they would hardly have needed a laboratory to believe it.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) explains how a person first comes to have a microbiome?
questions.explanation: Section C answers its own opening question, 'Where does this internal ecosystem come from?', by describing how a newborn acquires its first residents from birth, milk and the household.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) warns readers against commercial claims about gut health?
questions.explanation: Section D describes 'people eager to sell' the story, supplements that promise to 'restore' gut health, and diets marketed with more confidence than the science justifies.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) lists specific jobs that the gut's inhabitants perform for the body?
questions.explanation: Section B says the microbes 'earn their keep' and lists what they do: breaking down fibres, manufacturing vitamins and training the immune system.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) argues that the weaknesses of the research show it is immature rather than dishonest?
questions.explanation: Section E opens with 'None of this makes the field a fraud; it makes it young', which is exactly the contrast between dishonesty and immaturity.

questions.q: Which of the following best states the writer's overall position?
options: Antibiotics have done more damage to human health than any other medicine.
Research on mice has proved that gut bacteria determine mood and sleep.
A healthy microbiome can be restored with the right supplements and diet.
The microbiome is genuinely important, but claims about controlling it run far ahead of the evidence.
questions.explanation: Sections A–C establish that the microbes matter; sections D–E insist the science is young and that anyone 'claiming to command it' should be treated warily. The other options are either overstated or contradicted in section D.

questions.q: What does the writer's remark about great-grandparents at the end of section E suggest?
options: Laboratory research into the microbiome is a waste of money.
Vegetables grown in the past contained more vitamins than modern ones.
The most reliable advice the science currently offers is something people already accepted long ago.
Earlier generations enjoyed better health than people do today.
questions.explanation: The writer calls the supported advice 'unglamorous' and then notes that great-grandparents 'would hardly have needed a laboratory to believe it' — the point being that the science confirms old common sense rather than revealing anything new. Nothing is said about past health or past vegetables, and section E explicitly defends the field.

questions.q: In section D, the phrase 'groan under' is closest in meaning to
options: collapse beneath
are heavily loaded with
are emptied of
complain loudly about
questions.explanation: Shelves that 'groan under' supplements are so full that they seem to creak with the weight — an idiom for being heavily loaded. The literal 'complain' and 'collapse' do not fit shelves in a shop.

questions.q: According to the passage, the first thousand days of life are the only period during which the microbiome can be changed.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: Section C calls the first thousand days a window in which the microbiome is 'unusually open to influence', not the only such period, and section B shows that a course of antibiotics can change it much later in life.

passages.title: The Vanishing Hand
passages.passage:
There is a drawer in most family homes that nobody opens very often. [1] Read one today and the striking thing is not what it says but how it looks: the slope of the letters, the pressure of the pen, the small flourish under a signature. A page in a familiar hand carries its writer into the room in a way that no typed message can.

That such pages are becoming rarer is beyond dispute. Surveys across several countries find that a majority of adults have not written anything longer than a shopping list in the past month, and a substantial minority cannot recall the last time they wrote a full paragraph by hand. [2] Their essays are typed, their notes are photographed, and the cursive script that their grandparents laboured over is, in more than one education system, no longer taught at all.

To some, the trend is nothing to mourn. Handwriting, they point out, was never the point; it was merely the technology available for getting thoughts onto a surface, and technologies are replaced. Nobody weeps for the quill. [3] What matters, on this view, is that ideas are recorded and shared, and the keyboard does that faster, more legibly and for more people than the pen ever did.

Yet a body of research has begun to complicate this cheerful account. Children who learn their letters by forming them, rather than by pressing keys, appear to recognise those letters sooner and to read more fluently. Students who take notes by hand tend to remember more of a lecture than those who type, and not, as one might guess, because they write more down. [4] The slowness of the pen, in other words, is not a defect to be engineered away but the very mechanism by which the mind is made to work on what it hears.

None of this will bring the letter-writing drawer back into daily use, nor should it. [5] The sensible course is to treat handwriting as we treat mental arithmetic: a skill we no longer depend on for everyday business, but one whose disappearance would leave something in the mind a little weaker than before.

A. It is there that the letters are kept — from a grandmother, from a friend abroad, from a parent who is no longer alive.
B. Among the young, the figures are starker still.
C. It is precisely because they cannot keep up that they are forced to select, compress and rephrase, and it is this processing that fixes the material in memory.
D. Printing, the argument runs, was greeted with the same alarm, and it hardly ruined civilisation.
E. Few of them, it turned out, could name a single letter they had received in the past year.
F. The keyboard, after all, is here to stay, and a child who cannot type fluently is at a real disadvantage.
G. Doctors, whose handwriting was once a byword for illegibility, have been the first to welcome the change.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [2]?
questions.explanation: The sentence before gives figures for adults; 'Among the young, the figures are starker still' moves to a new group, and the next sentence's 'their essays', 'their notes' and 'their grandparents' can only refer to the young. E looks tempting but leaves 'their grandparents' without a sensible referent.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [3]?
questions.explanation: 'Nobody weeps for the quill' is one example of a replaced technology; D adds printing as a second, and 'the argument runs' keeps us inside the view of the people who think the trend is 'nothing to mourn'.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [4]?
questions.explanation: The sentence before denies that hand-writers remember more 'because they write more down'; C supplies the real reason — they cannot keep up, so they must process what they hear — and the following sentence sums this up as 'the slowness of the pen'.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [5]?
questions.explanation: F explains why the drawer should not return to daily use — the keyboard 'is here to stay' — and its 'after all' justifies the 'nor should it' just before. The next sentence then proposes the balanced 'sensible course'.

questions.q: What is the main point the writer makes about handwriting?
options: Schools should stop teaching typing until children can write cursive script.
Letters written by hand are more emotionally powerful than typed messages.
It should be kept alive as a skill because of what it does for the mind, even though it is no longer needed for daily tasks.
It is a dying technology that deserves no more sympathy than the quill.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph states the position directly: handwriting is like mental arithmetic, no longer depended on but worth keeping. The quill view is the one the writer 'complicates', and the emotional power of letters is only the opening illustration.

questions.q: What does the writer imply about those who say the decline of handwriting is 'nothing to mourn'?
options: They have a financial interest in the sale of keyboards.
They secretly regret the loss of handwriting themselves.
They have misread the research on note-taking.
Their argument is coherent but does not tell the whole story.
questions.explanation: The writer presents their view fairly and calls it a 'cheerful account' that research 'has begun to complicate' — that is, it is not wrong so much as incomplete. Since the research is described as new, they cannot be accused of misreading it, and no motive is attributed to them.

questions.q: In paragraph 2, 'laboured over' is closest in meaning to
options: worked hard at
complained about
quickly abandoned
quietly admired
questions.explanation: To labour over something is to put slow, effortful work into it; the grandparents spent hours practising cursive script. The contrast is with the young, whose essays are simply typed.

questions.q: Cursive script is still taught in every education system the passage refers to.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says cursive script is, 'in more than one education system, no longer taught at all', which directly contradicts the statement.

passages.title: The Pale Line on the Rock
passages.passage:
A. Anyone who has stood at the foot of a mountain glacier will have noticed the line. Above it the rock is dark, lichen-covered and weathered; below it, pale and raw, as if scrubbed. That line marks how high the ice reached within living memory, and in most valleys of the world it now sits a dizzying distance above the ice itself. Glaciers have advanced and retreated throughout the planet's history, but what the pale rock records is a retreat of a speed and scale that the geological archive struggles to match.

B. A glacier is best understood not as a frozen object but as a slow river with a budget. Snow that falls on its upper reaches is compressed into ice and flows downhill under its own weight; at the lower end, the ice melts. So long as the two roughly balance, the glacier holds its ground. Tip the balance — a little less snow in winter, a few more warm days in summer — and the front begins to withdraw. What makes the process so hard to reverse is that a shrinking glacier exposes darker ground, which absorbs more heat, which speeds the melting further. The ice, in effect, helps to write its own obituary.

C. Nowhere are the consequences felt more directly than in the mountain communities that have long treated glaciers as reservoirs. In the dry months, meltwater is what keeps rivers flowing, fields irrigated and turbines turning. Paradoxically, retreat brings a temporary abundance: for a few decades, a shrinking glacier releases more water than it stores, and the valleys below enjoy a windfall. Hydrologists call the moment when that flow begins to fall "peak water", and for many ranges it has either arrived or is not far off. Whatever comes after it will have to be managed by people who have never known scarcity.

D. The retreat also leaves behind hazards of a kind that few communities are prepared for. Meltwater pools behind walls of loose rubble left by the ice, forming lakes that can burst without warning and send a wall of water down a valley in minutes. Slopes that were held together by ice for millennia are freed to slide. Several countries have begun draining the most dangerous of these lakes, an expensive and delicate business, but the number of them grows faster than the budgets set aside to deal with them.

E. It is tempting to look at all this and ask how the ice can be saved. The honest answer is that, for most small glaciers, it cannot; the warming already locked into the system will see them gone within a lifetime whatever is done now. What remains within reach is more modest and more urgent: securing the water that the ice once secured, moving the villages that stand in the path of the lakes and, above all, ensuring that the great ice sheets of the far north and south, whose fate depends on decisions not yet taken, do not follow the same pale line down the rock.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) explains why the retreat of a glacier tends to speed up once it has begun?
questions.explanation: Section B describes the feedback loop: a shrinking glacier 'exposes darker ground, which absorbs more heat, which speeds the melting further'.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) describes a benefit of glacier retreat that will not last?
questions.explanation: Section C calls the extra meltwater a 'temporary abundance' and a 'windfall' lasting 'a few decades', after which the flow begins to fall.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) mentions a visible sign of how far the ice has already withdrawn?
questions.explanation: Section A describes the pale line on the rock that 'marks how high the ice reached within living memory' and now sits far above the ice.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) states that some of the loss can no longer be prevented?
questions.explanation: Section E says that most small glaciers cannot be saved, because 'the warming already locked into the system will see them gone within a lifetime whatever is done now'.

questions.q: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Draining glacial lakes is the most effective way to protect villages from flooding.
Glacier retreat is fast, largely irreversible for small glaciers, and its human consequences must now be managed rather than prevented.
Mountain communities have benefited from glacier retreat and should welcome the extra water.
Glaciers have always advanced and retreated, so the current retreat is nothing unusual.
questions.explanation: The passage moves from the scale of the retreat (A), through why it accelerates (B) and what it does to water supply and safety (C, D), to the conclusion that saving small glaciers is impossible and managing the consequences is what remains (E). Option 3 is contradicted in section A; the others are single details.

questions.q: What does the writer imply with the words 'people who have never known scarcity' at the end of section C?
options: The communities will be poorly prepared for the shortage because recent decades of abundance have hidden the problem.
The mountain communities are wealthier than those in the lowlands.
The coming shortage will turn out to be milder than the hydrologists predict.
Younger people manage water more carefully than their parents did.
questions.explanation: Section C has just explained that retreat brings a temporary windfall; the closing sentence points out that those who must manage the decline have only ever known that windfall. The implication is a lack of experience and preparation, not wealth or skill.

questions.q: In section C, the word 'windfall' is closest in meaning to
options: a sudden storm
a serious shortage
a long-term investment
an unexpected gain
questions.explanation: A windfall is a piece of good fortune that arrives without effort; here it is the extra water released by the shrinking glacier. The context — 'temporary abundance' — rules out shortage or investment.

questions.q: The writer believes that the great polar ice sheets are already beyond saving.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: Section E says the fate of the ice sheets 'depends on decisions not yet taken' and urges that they be prevented from following the small glaciers — so the writer regards them as still within reach, unlike most small glaciers.

passages.title: Sixty-Four Squares
passages.passage:
Few games can claim to be played, in something close to their present form, on every inhabited continent. Chess can, and the ease with which a player from one country sits down opposite a stranger from another disguises how long and improbable the game's journey has been. [1] The board it was played on had sixty-four squares, all of one colour, and the pieces on it were not a king and queen but a rajah and his adviser, flanked by elephants, horses, chariots and foot soldiers — an army, in short, of the kind that fought on the plains of the region.

From there the game travelled west along the trade routes, and with each border it crossed, it was quietly translated. [2] The elephant, an animal few of them had seen, was reimagined first as a bishop's mitre and, in some places, as a jester or a ship. The chariot, its purpose forgotten, became a tower. Only the horse, which needed no explanation anywhere, kept its shape.

The most consequential change of all came late and, as far as anyone can tell, in a single generation. [3] Almost overnight, a slow game of manoeuvre became one of ambush and sudden collapse, and the manuals written under the old rules were rendered obsolete. Historians still debate what prompted the change; that it coincided with the reign of several powerful queens in Europe has struck more than one of them as unlikely to be an accident.

[4] Coffee-house players of the eighteenth century would have recognised the board their descendants play on, but not the clocks, the written notation or the ranking systems that now surround it. The game as an organised sport, with its championships and its ratings, is a creation of the last hundred and fifty years, younger than the railway.

What survives across all these transformations is the underlying grammar: two equal forces, no dice, no hidden information and no luck beyond the order in which one's opponent makes mistakes. [5] That, more than any piece or rule, may be why a game invented to model one kind of warfare has outlived every army it was meant to represent.

A. The adviser, a modest piece that could shuffle only a single diagonal step, was transformed into the queen, the most powerful piece on the board, able to sweep its whole length and breadth.
B. Persian players, who received it first, kept the general shape but renamed the pieces in their own tongue; the Arabs, who took it from them, carried it as far as Spain; and the Europeans who inherited it there set about redrawing the pieces to match a world of castles and clergy.
C. Its earliest traceable ancestor emerged in northern India some fourteen centuries ago, under a name that meant "four divisions of the army".
D. Whoever plays it is stripped of every excuse, and the appeal of a contest in which the only variable is the quality of one's own thinking appears to be very nearly universal.
E. The Vikings, by contrast, took the game north and appear to have played it largely for money.
F. Nor did the modern game arrive all at once, even after the rules had settled.
G. The board itself, meanwhile, has never once been altered in all that time.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [1]?
questions.explanation: The gap must introduce where the 'journey' began; C names the origin and the old name, and the next sentence's 'the board it was played on' and 'rajah', 'elephants' and 'chariots' all follow naturally from an Indian ancestor.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [2]?
questions.explanation: B spells out the westward route and ends with Europeans 'redrawing the pieces'; the next sentence, 'an animal few of them had seen', needs those Europeans as its referent. E mentions a direction but breaks the chain and has no 'them' to supply.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [3]?
questions.explanation: The paragraph promises 'the most consequential change of all' and later mentions 'powerful queens'; A describes the adviser becoming the queen, which explains why a slow game became one 'of ambush and sudden collapse'.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [5]?
questions.explanation: D comments on the 'grammar' just described — no dice, no hidden information, no luck — by noting that the player 'is stripped of every excuse', and the following 'That … may be why' refers back to this universal appeal. G contradicts paragraph 1, which says the board was once all one colour.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How chess changed as it travelled across cultures, and what has stayed constant beneath those changes.
Why the queen is the most powerful piece on the chessboard.
The role of powerful European queens in the history of the game.
How chess became an organised sport with clocks and ratings.
questions.explanation: Each paragraph follows a stage of the game's journey and its transformations, and the final paragraph names what 'survives across all these transformations'. The queen, the European monarchs and the sporting apparatus are individual stages, not the whole.

questions.q: What does the writer suggest about the link between the queen's new powers and the powerful queens of Europe?
options: The change was actually made in Asia rather than in Europe.
It is a plausible explanation that has not been proved.
It has been rejected by every serious historian.
The monarchs themselves ordered the rules to be changed.
questions.explanation: The writer says historians 'still debate' the cause, and only that the coincidence 'has struck more than one of them as unlikely to be an accident' — a cautious suggestion, not a settled fact. Nothing supports the monarchs giving orders or an Asian origin for this particular change.

questions.q: In paragraph 3, 'rendered obsolete' is closest in meaning to
options: sold cheaply
written down
made useless
translated again
questions.explanation: Something obsolete is out of date and no longer of use; manuals describing the old rules could not help anyone once the rules had changed. 'Rendered' here simply means 'made'.

questions.q: The chariot was turned into a tower because European players understood its role in battle.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the chariot changed 'its purpose forgotten' — the opposite of players understanding its role.
